questions.q: What does the wait type PAGEIOLATCH_SH specifically indicate?
options: A task is waiting for a data page to be physically read from disk into the buffer pool for shared (read) access
A task is waiting for a lock held by another session to be released
A task is waiting for a network round trip to the client to complete
A task is waiting for a memory grant to become available
questions.explain: PAGEIOLATCH_SH is the classic wait for a data page not currently in the buffer pool, being read from disk for shared access.

questions.q: Why is WRITELOG considered a direct measure of log-write latency?
options: Because every transaction commit requires a synchronous write to the transaction log, so WRITELOG time reflects exactly that hardening latency
Because WRITELOG only occurs during full database backups
Because WRITELOG measures how long SELECT queries take to return
Because WRITELOG is unrelated to transaction commits
questions.explain: Log writes are synchronous by design and required for every commit, making WRITELOG time a direct signal of log-write latency.

questions.q: What does sys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats add beyond instance-wide wait stats?
options: It identifies exactly which physical database file (data or log) is accumulating read/write I/O stalls, with cumulative stall milliseconds per file
It shows which user is currently connected to each database
It replaces the need to ever look at wait statistics
It only reports on tempdb, never user databases
questions.explain: sys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats gives per-file granularity, letting you pinpoint the specific data or log file behind an instance-wide I/O wait category.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is generally NOT the right fix for a high WRITELOG wait total?
options: Adding more data-file storage spindles
Reducing transaction size and frequency (fewer, larger commits)
Moving the transaction log to faster or dedicated storage
Checking whether autogrowth events are stalling writers mid-workload
questions.explain: WRITELOG is tied to the log file specifically; data-file spindles are a separate storage volume and don't address log-write latency.

questions.q: A server shows a PAGEIOLATCH_SH spike. Per this lesson, which of the following is NOT automatically the correct conclusion?
options: The only possible fix is to buy faster physical disks
The buffer pool might be too small for the working set
A missing index might be forcing scans that read far more pages than necessary
It could be a legitimate large read from a report query that has to touch disk
questions.explain: The lesson stresses correlating wait evidence with per-file stats and running queries before concluding hardware is the cause — buffer pool sizing or missing indexes are often the real fix.
